copy.framing: Two ways to partner — a genuine choice. Puget Sound fields the deepest public water-transit operator bench in the country, with port and city partners alongside.
copy.enable_track: Grant landing access at existing piers and marina berths and a permitting pathway for a pilot corridor. Private capital finances the fleet; privately committed employer demand fills the seats. The ask is access, not money.
copy.operate_track: Washington's public bodies already own and operate ferry fleets — the state system, a county water taxi, and sales-tax-funded fast ferries. One is already funding design of an electric hydrofoil. Navier vessels can be procured the way transit vessels are procured — to build, run, or augment the public water network.

copy.headline: Your speed rules were written for boats that make wake.
copy.framing: Harbor speed rules exist to control wake, wash, noise, and disturbance — outcomes a foiling, electric Navier satisfies inherently.
copy.ask: Our ask: measure us. Where independent wake and noise measurement shows the rule's purpose is served, grant route-specific relief.

expander.title: What speed-rule relief unlocks
body: Seattle's own harbor code already draws the right distinction: it caps speed near shorelines, piers, and moorages, and it separately holds every operator liable for wake damage regardless of speed. The buffer numbers were calibrated for hulls that push wake; the wake rule states the actual purpose.
Our ask: measure us. Where independent wake and noise measurement shows the rule's purpose is served, align the number with the rule's purpose — route by route.

The strongest precedent is local: a foil-assisted low-wake catamaran was purpose-built to run wake-sensitive Rich Passage at speed after beach-monitoring studies, and it operates daily. Stockholm's transport authority runs an electric hydrofoil at roughly twice a posted zone speed under a low-wake exemption.

rule_basis.detail: 7 knots within 200 yards of any shoreline/pier in city waters (Elliott Bay); 3 knots inside marinas per 16.20.130.F; lowest max controls
rule_basis.source: Seattle City Clerk archived SMC Title 16 (re-verify on Municode before quoting externally, per SPEED-RULES-SEATTLE.md §6)

rule_basis.detail: compliance with speed limits does not exempt wake-damage liability — Seattle separates the numeric cap from the outcome rule
negligent-operation standard accounting for vessel-wake effects; no numeric cap on open water

_provenance.relief_pathway_honesty: No exemption mechanism is visible in SMC 16.20.130 (unlike Massachusetts' marked-channel permission) — so the rendered ask deliberately does NOT claim an existing mechanism; relief would run through City action, the county council, or the COTP depending on the instrument. Rendered copy names no instrument numbers.

navier_intro.title: Meet the vessel

copy.headline: Zero-emission. Near-silent. Almost no wake.
copy.subline: Navier is a U.S. builder of electric hydrofoil vessels — the traits that matter for harbor rules and harbor neighbors are built into the hull, not bolted on.
copy.body: The N45 Explorer carries 30 passengers at a foilborne cruise speed of about 20 knots, lifted clear of the water for a smooth, wake-free ride. The smaller N30 Quanta carries 8. Foiling cuts energy use by up to ~90% versus a conventional planing hull, and both vessels run near-silent on electric power.

reference.title: Reference

copy.intro: The region's water-transportation landscape — Puget Sound and Lake Washington — spans state, county, port, and municipal bodies. We seek conversations — nothing here implies approval, endorsement, or commitment by any body named.

bodies.role: Operates the largest US ferry system — 19.1M riders in 2024 — and is committed to fleet electrification; its terminals sit beside two stations on this network.
Runs the King County Water Taxi from Pier 50 downtown and the Seacrest Park dock in West Seattle — this network's West Seattle station is its terminal.
Sales-tax-funded fast-ferry operator serving Bremerton, Kingston, and Southworth; running an FTA-funded electric-hydrofoil research program with $5.2M of state design and prototype funding.
The four-county region's planning council; ran the Puget Sound Passenger-Only Ferry Study assessing new routes region-wide.
Owns Bell Harbor Marina — the only marina in downtown Seattle and this network's downtown gate; its Century Agenda pairs maritime innovation with emissions reduction.

bodies.body: City of Seattle (SDOT, Parks, Harbor Patrol)
bodies.role: Permitting and landing access in city waters; Seattle Parks controls the Seacrest dock; Harbor Patrol enforces the harbor code.

The county authority on Lake Washington's waters — county boating rules set the shore-buffer standard across the lake; posted low-speed zones near shore apply, and the open lake crossing is unrestricted.
Owns the Bellevue Marina at Meydenbauer Bay — this network's Bellevue gate; a posted low-speed zone applies near shore and inside the bay.
Owns Marina Park's city dock and moorage in downtown Kirkland — this network's Kirkland station, with Carillon Point Marina to the south as the second Kirkland stop.
Owns Gene Coulon Memorial Beach Park and its day-moorage docks at the lake's south end — this network's Renton station, beside the Southport waterfront.
No station on the island; its police marine patrol serves the lake waters of several shoreline cities, and mid-lake transit past the island runs on open water under county rules.
Owns the 840-slip Des Moines Marina and ran its own Des Moines–Seattle passenger-ferry pilot in 2022 — on exactly the corridor this network serves.
Owns the Kingston marina and dock; has operated a passenger ferry of its own in the past — the conversation here is landing access with private capital, not port-underwritten service.
Captain of the Port — navigation safety and federal oversight for all commercial passenger operations on the Sound and Lake Washington.
